utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I usually leave the reading of decisions until the end but that goes until the moment where we really have to find time. Therefore, I'd like to start with giving the reasons for the Chamber's decision on protective measures for Witness JF-027. The Chamber has not yet communicated the reasons for its decision granting trial-related protective measures for Witness JF-027 which was delivered prior to the commencement of the witness's testimony on the 9th of November 2010 in private session and can be found at transcript page 8872. The Chamber will now give its reasons. On the 26th of October, 2004, Witness JF-027 was granted a pseudonym in this case. On the 14th of October, 2009, the Prosecution requested that the witness be granted the additional protective measures of image and voice distortion. On the 25th of November, 2009, the Stanisic Defence opposed the request, the Simatovic did not respond. On the 8th of November, 2010, the Prosecution filed a supplemental motion for protective measures requesting closed session testimony for Witness JF-027. On the 9th of November of that same year, the Stanisic Defence indicated that it did not object the request. The Simatovic Defence expressed a general concern with regard to the granting of protective measures but deferred to the Chamber's assessment. All of this can be found at transcript pages 8870 and 8871. The Chamber has set out in previous decisions the test it applies when considering whether to grant protective measures. In this respect, the Chamber refers the parties to the reasons for the decision to grant protective measures to Witness C-1118, which can be found at transcript pages 3690 through 3692. Witness JF-027 fears for his safety and that of his family if it were to become known that he is a witness in the current case. The evidence provided by the witness concerns operations and attacks of Arkan's Tigers, as well as the co-operation between Arkan's tiger, the Red Berets, the Serbian MUP and the VRS. His evidence implicates several former members of these units. The witness argues that he has received threats in the past, which could be renewed if it became known that he testified in this case. The witness moved abroad as a result of the threats. However, his family currently still resides in Republika Srpska. The Chamber found that the fact the witness would give evidence to the Tribunal might antagonise persons living in or with access to the area where his family resides. The Chamber considered the 37th report of the high representative for implementation of the peace agreement on Bosnia and Herzegovina report to the Secretary-General of the United Nations of the 19th of May, 2010, which reports the existence of an unstable security situation in the territory of the Republika Srpska, particularly unfavourable to witnesses who co-operate with the Tribunal. The Chamber also considered that the nature of Witness JF-027's testimony makes him easily identifiable for those familiar with the events about which he would testify. Considering all the above circumstances and balancing the risks that the witness and his family may face after testifying before the Tribunal and the accuseds' right to a public trial, the Chamber granted the requested protective measures. And this concludes the reasons for the Chamber's decision. The Prosecution has filed a request for leave to reply to the Defence responses to the Prosecution's second bar table motion, that is a request of the 1st of February. Is there any objection against granting it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Trial Chamber's instructions of the 18th of February, 2010, at this time I will present a public summary of the evidence of Witness JF-064. The witness has reviewed this summary and verified its contents. In April 1992, Serb forces took over Kljuc municipality and forced the witness and other Bosniaks in the municipality to perform work for the Serb forces, including at the front line. In May 1995, the Bosnian Serb military police picked up the witness and several other men from his village, took them to the front line, and forced them to carry out such dangerous tasks as trench digging and pulling the wounded from the battle-fields. After the Bosnian army had broken through the Serb forces line, on 19 September 1995, the witness and four of his neighbours were forced to go to Sanski Most with the VRS unit from Kljuc that they had been assigned to work for. When they got there, one of Arkan's Men required them to assist in the transfer of ammunition and equipment from the Veleprom warehouse to Hotel Sanus in Sanski Most. Witness JF-064 and his neighbours were taken into the Hotel Sanus where Arkan asked them for their names. Arkan then sent them into a narrow corridor where Arkan's Men verbally abused them, called them "Turks," and forced them to sit cross-legged with their heads to the ground for hours. At around 2.30 in the morning, Witness JF-064 and 11 others were handcuffed two-by-two and transported by some of Arkan's Men on a truck away from Hotel S anus to a place that the witness later learned was Trnova. The men were taken out two-by-two and the witness heard shots. All four of the neighbours from Kljuc exited the truck before the witness. When the witness came off the truck, Arkan's Men removed the handcuffs that bound him to another man that he did not know. They were ordered by one of Arkan's Men to enter a small room where the witness could already see bodies and pools of blood. As they entered the room, shots were fired. A bullet hit the witness and he fell to the ground. He remained lying still as Arkan's Men brought in the remaining men from the truck and shot them in the room. Arkan's Men slit the throat of one and the blood sprayed over the witness's face. The witness received two more non-fatal shots, a total of three shots. Once Arkan's Men had left him for dead, he escaped. JF-064 is the only surviving victim of the Trnova massacre which is discussed in paragraph 56 of the indictment.

To which you responded: "Four of them." You were asked if any were "close friends of yours." And you named Mehmed Sehic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would now like to ask Mr. Laugel to play an excerpt from Exhibit P170 beginning at the time stamp 3:30 and ending at 3:53. Please play this excerpt without sound and leave the final screen shot on the monitor for questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness JF-064, do you recognise where this video was filmed?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: This video was filmed in the garage, the one where I survived the execution in Trnova in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Are there any features visible from this video that would allow you to identify any of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I recognise my good friend, Mehmed Sehic. I recognise his top. I remember what he was wearing on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've testified that you were also shot here. Is the place where you fell visible on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is there any dispute about that it was left corner or the the right corner? I mean, is there any dispute at all about the, if I could say so, execution of a number of people which were detained?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we go into any further details, I mean, I didn't want to stop you, but we've seen that pictures are taken from the scene of where this horrible event happened, but to go into further detail if there's no dispute about it, might be unnecessary. And I'm also, of course, looking at the clock. You said you would need your half an hour, well, you took already more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just show the witness a still of this last screen shot and allow him to mark on it which man he identified as his friend and also where he fell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is there any dispute about that there was a friend of him among them and to know exactly which of the dead bodies was his friend seems, of course it's for the witness very important, but for the Chamber it doesn't make a lot of difference. And this is not a lack of interest in the Chamber, but these are details which are irrelevant for the determinations the Chamber has to make. Apparently, the Defence and the Chamber accepts that amongst the dead bodies seen on this photograph, which, of course, is a picture which one does not easily forget, that the friend of the witness is among them. Unless there's any specific reason why you would like to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In that case, I'll leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I hope you do understand that where everyone accepts the event that take place, that details as in which corner or you were, et cetera, for the Chamber it is -- these are not the details that are important, but that this event happened, that is important. You were there, your friend was there as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. I've one issue I'd like to take you back to and we should -- it should not be shown on the screen. That is 2123. Could we have a look at it. Again both original and translation, second page in the ... Could we have the original next to it. Last page. Could we zoom in on the last line of the text and the stamp below it. No, the other stamp, the stamp. There are three stamps, the middle one, and the text just above it. Yes. Could we zoom in even more. If I look at the translation, it says number 11 is the last one. What I see clearly on that line above the stamp is a number 3, which does not appear in any way in the translation. I also see a stamp being described as being of the lower court of Sanski Most. Now, my eyes hardly can read what it says. Apart from that, I read the word Bihac which is not in the translation and it's one of the few legible parts, so I was a bit surprised by this translation together with this original.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will look into this at the break and report back, and, if necessary, we could have it -- the translation submitted for -- to be verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it -- of course, it suggests this number 11 was the last one, that it's a more extensive document. But let's -- we'd like to hear from you. Who is going to be the first to cross-examine the witness? It will be you. Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock, wouldn't it be a better idea if you would start cross-examination after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy with that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might then use a couple of minutes for another matter but not necessarily in the presence of the witness. We'll take a break, witness. If you could perhaps already follow the usher and we'd like to see you back in approximately half an hour where you will be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one matter I would like to briefly raise with you, Mr. Jordash. The Chamber has received a submission in which you were asking to -- well, to deal with the -- I would say, the financial matter with the Registry, that's one. But also to suspend all the proceedings apart from the examination of the remaining Prosecution witnesses. It's not entirely clear what you mean by suspend all the proceedings, whether that, for example, would also include any time-limits already set or that we, in your view, are supposed not to set any further time-limits. That's not entirely clear to us. That's one. Second, the Chamber has received a copy of a letter which is not yet considered in your submission and, of course, the Chamber would like to know to what extent that letter changes anything, if only the urgency of the requests you have made. The Chamber would like, not necessarily at this moment, but if you could say something about it either now or tomorrow or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm not sure what letter Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About additional funding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was that from the Registry to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To all counsel, I think. To all Defence counsel, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask when it's dated, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have seen until now a rather lengthy explanation, whereas I'm referring to, let me see, 28th of January, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, the 28th of January, 2011, letter is dealt with in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's the long one. Is that the same date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a one-and-a-half page letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is something different then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I read one line to you so then "therefore in order to ensure continued funding during trial proceedings, and in light of the expected end of the Prosecution phase of trial in mid-February," and then I leave out a few words between brackets, "the Registry proposes to make available the regular monthly stipend to your respective teams" so that's both for you and Simatovic, "for the month of February 2011."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That, I think, is a letter which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's for the both teams. It's addressed "all lead counsel Stanisic and Simatovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps you read it first and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You haven't seen that. It might be relevant, perhaps from only the part, as I said whether it changes anything, if only the immediate urgency. Please have a look at it and please think about both suspension, what it exactly means in this context, and whether this changes, perhaps not on a long term, but perhaps on the short term anything. We'll have a break and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Jordash, there may have been some confusion about the 28th of January letters and to what extent it was included in submissions. It certainly was not in your oral submissions. Now, I didn't go in detail through the submissions and all the annexes, but rather roughly, and it may be, I do understand that there was some confusion about what was annexed in that later submission and I do understand that even the short 28th of January letter was also an annex to your last submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it wasn't intended to be. The only 28th of January letter I had seen, has now, I hope, been sent to Your Honours. That was -- it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The long one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the long one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This one I hadn't seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You hadn't seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the confusion is complete but look at everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've seen it, I'm in a position when Your Honours wish for me to address you on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-064, you'll now be cross-examined by Defence counsel Mr. Jordash, counsel for Mr. Stanisic. He is the Defence lawyer who will first cross-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I only have a very few questions for you. May I start by expressing my and my client's sympathy for your terrible experience. I'm not seeking to challenge the truthfulness of your account. We accept it happened and we accept it was horrific. But I do want to ask you some few details just to clarify a few points. Now, you've spoken about Arkan's Men, some wearing black caps, some wearing red berets. The men who were wearing red berets, were those red berets the same as Arkan's red beret?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Indicating that they were members of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: What is SDG? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, did they have the same insignia as Arkan's beret?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And their role when you saw them was to bring in those who were being engaged in work conscription such as yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: They didn't bring in just us, but also all other non-Serbs from Sanski Most. They had a local Serb with them and they praise him to Arkan as somebody who was very familiar with the area who was familiar with every house, every step, every road. In other words, they brought in all non-Serb citizens of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the men wearing black caps, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I don't know what they were doing but while we were standing in the corridor of the hotel, I saw them on a number of occasions, either coming up or down the stairs. In any case, they always seemed to respect very strict discipline. They walked in a single file very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The local Serbs who were assisting Arkan's Men, were they members of a military force, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: There was just that one man who wore a uniform of the reserve police. I am familiar with the appearance of that uniform because before the war I was also a member of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this was a uniform of the reserve police from where?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: The reserve police of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just moving forward a little. When you were taken towards the site that became the execution site, were you under the impression you were being taken in the usual way to work?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: No, that was not my impression because we had been handcuffed. Had we not have been handcuffed, maybe that would have been my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at what point were you handcuffed? Were you handcuffed at the hotel or sometime after that?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: In front of the hotel before we were loaded on to the truck, and then in Trnova when we got off the truck and when we reached that little room where we would eventually be executed, that's where they took our handcuffs off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you were handcuffed, were other civilians being taken off to work from the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I don't know what work are you referring to. We were handcuffed and we were taken to be executed. What happened next, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know where Arkan was when you were handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: We were standing there with heads cast down, behind us there was a soldier who cocked his rifle and he had been ordered to shoot if any one of us moved, so we really could not observe the situation to see who was where in that part of the corridor. But before that, Arkan was at the very entrance to the hotel. There was a door to the left, he had just come out of the room behind that door the first time we saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know if he would have been able to see you being handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I believe that nothing could happen among his army, if I may call it that, without his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But do you think he saw you being handcuffed? What I'm trying to get at, Mr. Witness, before you answer, is whether you have any information as to whether this was ordered by Arkan or was the men involved going on a frolic of their own?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Not only did he see it, but he also ordered it a hundred per cent. I repeat, nothing happened unbeknownst to him without his approval. We had been known to wait for hours to unload ammunition or equipment until the moment he came back from the front line. Then you will understand what kind of discipline they observed. And also I overheard soldiers talking about awful things that happened to them if they did something of their own accord and how terribly they suffered. I can give you an example to illustrate what I've just said. They are ordered to do physical exercise while the others were ordered to beat them on the back with wooden sticks. I never said that before in any of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So what you've just described is what you recall happening over a number of days and weeks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I am speaking about what happened that evening, that night, what I personally experienced and saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you said, "We had been known to wait for hours to unload ammunition or equipment," so you were referring to that particular day?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I only have one follow-up question in this respect. You earlier when Mr. Jordash asked you whether you had any information as to whether this was ordered by Arkan or whether they may have done it on their own, you said: "Not only did he see it, but he ordered it as well." Now, the first: When you were handcuffed, did you observe Arkan was nearby as to see that you were handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The room where he was had a large window through which he could see the area where the truck was that we were loaded on to with our hands handcuffed. I can't state with a hundred per cent certainty that he saw us, but judging by everything I experienced that day and that night, I'm certain that nothing could be done without his approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. You would say they wouldn't do anything unless he would have approved or ordered it. Now, did you hear him order you to be handcuffed or is it a conclusion, rather, that it could not be anything else then that he ordered it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my assumption. I didn't hear it. I didn't see it. I assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, finally, I think part of your testimony was also that the soldiers said that if you would pay 5.000 Deutschemarks that you would be released. Did they specifically at that moment say Arkan will release you if you pay 5.000? It didn't happen, but did they mention Arkan specifically in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They said, You are lucky that you have been captured by Arkan's Soldiers. Tell us where your houses are, we'll get on to the truck and we'll get the money. Those were the words that they used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but they did not say that Arkan had decided that if you would come up with the money, that you would be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all, on behalf of my Defence team and my client, I would like to express my sympathy for the ordeal that you went through. I will not dwell on upon that. I just have a few brief questions about some other parts of your statement and your testimony so far. In your statement provided in 1996, which is P2112, in paragraph 6 you describe your arrival at the front line near Bihac in 1995, and you say in that part of your statement: "I noticed that all the equipment and weapons that were used by the Serbs belonged to the JNA." Could you please be more specific, what equipment and what weapons did you see in that part of the front line near Bihac on that occasion when you were taken there to work?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: All sorts of weapons. To be more specific, military trucks, Pinzgauers, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All the equipment that you saw, as far as you know, had belonged to the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also mentioned that you saw Arkan on TV?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you remember, as you sit here today, during the war what TV channel did you see him on and what did you see? Can we just concentrate on the war period, please.

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I watched often footage from some of the Croatian theatres of war where he was and apart from the war I was watching his electoral campaign spots because he had some sort of political party. And before the war he was the leader of the supporters of the Red Star football club, and I was also one of his supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you knew about Arkan even before the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P2125.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we saw this still a short while ago. Could you please tell us how you can tell that this is a unit led by Arkan based on this still because I suppose you were not able to see this live?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this live, but I am convinced that the man at the head of the column is Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher to hand you a pen so you can circle the face of the person you suppose is Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is there any reason to doubt that the witness earlier said in the front the man with the black? There's only one in the front, isn't it. Of course we could ask him, but could you circle it, the man you think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That appears on the record clearly from his previous testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us anything on the uniforms of these people that would show that they are members of that unit? Can you see any insignia that would help us make this conclusion? If you do, please circle it.

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I don't know what to circle because if I recognise Arkan in front, what is left for me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So apart from Arkan's face and there's nothing else to point to the identity of the unit?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I don't know who -- which other unit it could be led by him if not Arkan's tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this marked photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00220. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You said D00220, but that -- yes, it's a Defence exhibit. Yes, D220 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this terrible event happened at Trnova?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of the distance between Trnova and Sanski Most in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I think it's about a kilometre or one and a half kilometres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The place where the Kljuc unit of the VRS was, Poljak, how far is it from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: I think that the distance is about the same, only in a different direction, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the distance between Trnova and Poljak is about 3 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day before the event you described while you were in Sanski Most, were there times when you were under nobody's control when you could move about Sanski Most freely?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: The only time when we were under nobody's control was from the entry point to Sanski Most toward -- until the passage to Poljak. That was the only time because we were not supposed to be without anybody to guard us and escort us at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, after this event that you described, do you know when the BH Army entered Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: At the time I was in Tuzla already, but I think that it was in late October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Late October 1995?

utterances.speaker: JF-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Any -- could we ask you one thing: You referred to paragraph 6 of -- I think it was 2112 -- no, 2012. I have no paragraph numbers in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the B/C/S version of statement 2112, the paragraphs are marked by hand, but now I see that they are not marked in the same way in the English versions, but the paragraph I'm referring to is the last one on the first page in English, and it ends on the following page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how the numbering is but that's the page going over from the first page with content to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find -- I see in the previous paragraph that the witness noticed that all the equipment and weapons were used by the Serbs. That's in -- but then, let me see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the reference to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, Bihac -- or first of all, this is the last but one paragraph on the first page right there, and Bihac is mentioned halfway through the paragraph, after the names of persons and the following sentence Bihac is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just above Bihac. No, I had difficulties in finding it in the paragraph you earlier referred to, but it's clear to me now. Ms. Harbour, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no further questions for you, which means that this concludes your testimony, Witness 64. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench, questions about an experience which as all the parties have expressed, must have been a horrific experience for you. I thank you for coming and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness will testify with voice distortion which requires 10 minutes preparation. Therefore, we'll have a break of 10 minutes and then perhaps before the next break I do understand that you have -- that there are, Mr. Weber, half an hour is the estimate, isn't it? Examination-in-chief? No, no, it's only cross-examination, yes, I'd forgotten about that. Then we'll have a short break first but this is not the -- I take it it's still on the same tape so we'll have -- relatively soon after that we'll have another break. We'll resume in 10 minutes from now, but before we do so, I first have to put on the record what the basis is for what we are doing. On the 17th of December of last year, the Stanisic Defence filed a motion in which they requested a recall of Witness JF-047. On the 28th of December, the Prosecution filed its response in which it did not oppose the motion. The Chamber then decided to grant the request which was informally communicated to the parties in an e-mail dated January the 12th of this year, 2011, and the Chamber in that respect gave some further instructions to the parties such in relation to contact with the witness, for the witness not to speak or otherwise communicate with anyone else about his testimony, and a corresponding instruction for the Victims and Witness Section. In that e-mail, it is said that the decision will be put on the record at a later stage which is hereby done. We'll have a short break of 10 minutes. --- Break taken at 4.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. The witness will testify with pseudonym, face, and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Witness JF-047. Before you will give further evidence, I'd like to invite you to make again the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony when you were here earlier, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I read it? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-047, there were reasons for the Defence to ask this Chamber to be allowed to put further questions to you. The Chamber granted that request, and that's the reason why we asked you to come back to The Hague, as well have been communicated with you by the Victims and Witness Section. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to further cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be further cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. As you may remember, Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have, please, on the screen, 65 ter 6144.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd like to have you have a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just ask the document not be broadcast to the public. It's the witness's personal information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not to be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, this is the front first page of a document, and I would like to you read it and see if you recognise it just by looking at this page.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You do recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my personal information. This is probably from either my military booklet or from my military personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it says here "technical service."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you explain what that means and what connections you are making?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The connection I make is that the address mentioned here is that of my mother, and I lived there in 1978 or 1979 when I served in my compulsory military service in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But what is the significance, if anything, of the words "technical service," and why does that make you think that this probably came from your military booklet or military personnel file?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in Ljubljana I was in the technical service, in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page and have a look at not -- what it says. Please read through the document.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you enlarge it a bit, if possible. Thank you. Could you please scroll down. Thank you. Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when did you provide this statement and to whom?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we can see, can we not, that it's sometime after August of 1992 because there's reference to a date at the bottom which is August -- 27th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when I gave this statement or to who, but probably there is an indication of that on the statement itself, to who it was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You really have no recollection whatsoever of who you gave this statement to?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you in any way recall signing this statement, even if you don't recall anything else about it?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can believe me, I don't remember. I can see that some dates were changed, but I don't remember to who I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's have a look at its content. Looking two-thirds of the way down the statement, it says: "I stayed in Mlaka --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we should go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness JF-047, we'll take a break of again half an hour, and then some more questions will be put to you by the Prosecution, perhaps by the Defence and by the Bench as well, we'll see. We resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-047, you'll now be further examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber, as you may also remember, is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: JF-047, before you now is still Prosecution 6144, the first page of the exhibit. I'd like to direct your attention to the handwriting on this page. Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Could I add something about this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you just another question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall or do you know whose handwriting appears on this page?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: JF-047, is there something additional that you wish to add with respect to this document?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only now have I noticed an error in my year of birth in English. It says that I was born in 1955, and that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the original it's not any different. You see also in your own language, the handwriting is 1955, but that's a mistake, you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The date is correct, but the year when I was born is 1959. My eyesight is not very good anyway, I thought that this was a 9. Now that I have looked more carefully, I see that there is a mistake. I don't know where this document comes from. It's certainly not from the military department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since you've raised that matter, could you please review the rest of the personal information on here and indicate whether or not it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest is correct. I don't know my mother's a birth date, believe me, but the rest is correct. My specialty, my blood type. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the telephone number that appears in the entry for your mother, where does that telephone number belong to? What republic?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telephone number is correct, and it is in the Republic of Serbia. There was a time when the Republic of Serbia did have that telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have page 2 of 65 ter 6144.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: JF-047, the document that appears before you now is entitled "Biography." Before asking you some questions about the contents of this document, I'd like to ask you a very simple question: Do you know how to type?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot use a mechanical typewriter, I've never had one, but I can use a computer keyboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall who typed this biography?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do if this is the statement that I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will come back to that later on. I'd like you to review the first three paragraphs of this biography. It discusses your personal information and background. Is it correct that aside from your compulsory military service, that you resided and worked in Serbia prior to 1991 as stated in these first three paragraphs? If I could ask you to please refrain from referring to any particular locations since this document is not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the eighth line from the bottom of this note which references the training centre in Lezimir, is this training centre located in Serbia also?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The end of this note references two individuals. The names that are present are Crnog and Zivorad Ivanovic. Are these individuals the commanders that you were subordinated to as a member of the special purpose unit of the MUP Serbia, which you previously testified to?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the reference to Crnog, is this the same individual that you previously testified is Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this reference to Zivorad Ivanovic a reference to the same person that you previously testified to as being known as Zika Crnogorac?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the sixth line from the bottom, this biography indicates you had a serial number. Do you recall what this serial number represents?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got these serial numbers on plaques that were distributed to us before we left for Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "we got these serial numbers on plaques" that were distributed to you, who did you receive these serial numbers from?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the uniforms, serial numbers, and all that were things we received at a Pajzos before leaving for Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And while you were at Pajzos, who provided with you the serial numbers?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who it was individually, but it was the unit commander who distributed them to us. But of course, I don't know who -- I can't say who manufactured those plaques.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say the unit commander, what unit are you referring to that you were part of at that time in Pajzos? I believe you previously testified to this.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srecko Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the time in Pajzos, is that when you were a member of the special purpose unit of the MUP Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a few days before we were transferred from Lezimir to Pajzos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've just referred to plaques. Could you please describe to us what plaques you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are actually two plaques. They are the same kind as worn by American soldiers with the personal information. On ours there was the first name and the last name as well as a serial number. I can't remember if there was anything else on them. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 7626 of your previous testimony on the 4th of October, 2010, between lines 16 and 18, you stated: "We were told that we should leave all our identification papers behind, whoever had their IDs on them or military booklets. We had been given tags a couple of days before." JF-047, my question to you is: Was this serial number used or present on your tags or any of your IDs while you were a member of the special purpose unit of the MUP Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the tag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the two documents that you've shown -- been shown here today, have you seen these documents -- with respect to the second one, apologise. With respect to the second document, have you seen this document since you signed it?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. Last year or the year before, if we are talking about the statement that I gave to the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were previously shown two statements by the Serbian -- or involving members of the Serbian Radical Party when you were previously here. These were Exhibits D122 and D123 marked for identification. Are those the only two statements that you provided to the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave a couple of statements. This last one, if I may explain, the one that you've just showed, I can explain how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you do that, I'd like to ask you, you were brought back here today and shown these documents. You are indicating that you have not seen these documents since you signed it. Do you have any clear recollection about when or to whom this biography was provided to?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tell you, I'm not sure. Last year or the year before, and before that I gave a biography but that was merely a biography and I gave it to Ljubisa Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I may have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did though, just from -- although I have no further questions, the Prosecution would like to tender this exhibit into evidence, 65 ter 6144, and we'd also like to tender the RFA that was received pursuant which we've uploaded as 65 ter 6145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac is nodding yes already. Mr. Jordash, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objections of the statement, but there is an objection to the tendering of the RFA. The RFA -- well, I don't know if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we discuss that because I take it that the RFA is not a matter on which anyone would like to ask questions and hear the answers of this witness on the RFA, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, we just wanted to alert the Chamber to the fact that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll consider that we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, we have 6144, which is the -- as a matter of fact, the April and undated result of the result of the RFA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P02126, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2126 is admitted under seal. The other one, that is the RFA, 65 ter 6145, should be marked for identification under seal, or is there no need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also under seal. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P02127 marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-047, in the biography, it says that since you went to Bosnia -- let me find. Since you left from Bosnia you served as a special purpose unit member of the MUP Krajina combat group Bosanski Samac with that serial number. Did you ever apply for a job with the MUP Krajina? Did you -- when you left for Bosnia, did you ever apply for being a member of the MUP Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From earlier answers you gave when you were here in October, it sounded as if it should be hidden, more or less, who you were and where you came from. Was that the case when you left for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any moment that you received information that you were supposed to present yourself as a member of the MUP Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because let me be quite clear with you, of course it is puzzling why in that biography it is said that you served as a member of the MUP Krajina where you here say that you did not.

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement, if I may explain, the statement that was shown here, was given to a member of the Serb Radical Party for a monograph that was supposedly going to be written about the participation of volunteers, and so on. And, yes, it just occurred to me that this statement has neither a signature nor a stamp. There's only my signature on it. I'm not saying that I didn't give the statement, but much has been altered here. Well, not much, but this thing about Krajina, never in my life did I state ever anywhere that I was a member of the Krajina MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you give some details about giving this statement, whereas earlier when Mr. Jordash asked you questions about it, you didn't remember anything at all. What makes it that you are now suddenly able to tell us that it was given to a member of the Serb Radical Party, and as you add now, for a mono-graph?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to remember how a statement on a single page could have appeared without a signature or a stamp but saying in the letterhead that it was the Krajina MUP. I did give it a thought, and I concluded that this was the only possible explanation. Up there it says that it's the Krajina MUP, but where is the stamp of that MUP? I've never been to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you were examined in October, quite a lot was said about the payments you had received, the two payments you said that were brought in. Do you have any recollection as to payments coming from the MUP Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only money that I received later was money from the Republika Srpska, but that was in late 1992. That was not in the period while I was a member of this unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said you received it from the Republika Srpska. For what reason did you receive money from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money that I received in May and June and in August, actually, in June and August, was money from the Republic of Serbia. Later, when I returned to the Republika Srpska, then as a member their unit, I received money from Republika Srpska. They gave us some money for cigarettes and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And their unit, could you be a bit more specific what you exactly refer to when you said "as a member of their unit"?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the brigade or special purposes brigade of the MUP of Serbia. That was until I was wounded and later in the period after my injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said you received money from the Republika Srpska as a member of their unit. In your answer, you are referring to a brigade or a special purposes brigade of the MUP of Serbia which is not the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the latter half of 1992. Actually, the third -- third of 1992. Then I was a member of the VRS. I was a volunteer. Then I had no longer anything to do with the unit from Serbia. That's the period after my wounding and the period after Zivorad Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have no further questions for you. Any further questions, Mr. Jordash, Mr. Bakrac? Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave and given the fact that we have time, I have two or three questions that stem from the examination by Mr. Weber and your questions, so I have two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Weber asked you whether you had left all your personal ID at Pajzos before you left for Bosnia and you answered that you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was the reason why you left all your personal ID at Pajzos and went to Bosnia only with these tags?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One reason was that if we should get killed or taken prisoner, that our personal ID shouldn't become known and that the fact that the unit had come from Serbia wouldn't become known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very good. We are now in open session, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The first document we showed to you was dated 10 April, 1992. And you said that it was drafted at Batkusa; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My colleague will check that. Where were you on 10th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Batkusa, but I didn't say that the document was drafted there. I was at Batkusa on the 10th of April, 1992, but the document wasn't drafted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know where it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that I supposed it was drafted in the draft department. I have just checked now and seen that my date of birth is indicated as 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You said that you had to be completely incognito, but here we see your full personal ID with your mother's name and phone number and the date 10th of April, 1992. So my question is: Where were you on that date?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Batkusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is Batkusa in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and is the 10th of April a date after your departure from Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. And another question. I've already asked you, but I must ask you some more. Mr. Srecko Radovanovic at the time was one of the more prominent member of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you gave this statement for a mono-graph of the Serb Radical Party, wouldn't Srecko Radovanovic, who knows your military past very well, wouldn't he be able to establish that you are the -- the information in your biography is false?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Srecko Radovanovic took it. He may have never seen this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you you think that somebody, while compiling a mono-graph of the Serbian Radical Party, would take your biography but leave out that of the Srecko Radovanovic? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: JF-047 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Have the questions of the bench for the new questions from Mr. Bakrac triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we came at a point where we can establish that this concludes your testimony. I hope, Witness JF-047, that we'll not be in another round after this one. I'd like to thank you very much for coming again and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a couple of minutes left. Mr. Jordash, you earlier indicated that you could say a few words about the matter I raised earlier, I think. If that's the case, we could hear that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Having read the second letter dated the 28th of January, 2011, our position remains the same. The letter appears to say two things. One, that the Registry is prepared to look at the recess periods having consulted with the Chamber, and we in the Defence are grateful for Your Honours' information that has been passed to OLAD, but OLAD's position is once again, in our submission, extremely conditional. A promise to consider one of the issues which we've raised in the motion, but no firm commitment concerning what that actually means in real terms. And whether that will alter the position that we are in which is a co-counsel short. And the second part of the letter is again what we referred to in the motion as effectively taking what already belongs to us and handing it back to us and representing it as somehow new funding. It's this end-of-stage payment which is 20 per cent taken off our remuneration, moved to the end of the phase, and what OLAD are saying is, Well, we are going to take that money which you have already earned and we are going to give it to you a bit earlier than you would have got it anyway. That, in our submission, is a completely unacceptable and unhelpful mechanism for solving this problem. So our position remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that this letter doesn't save the problem as a whole for you. That's clear. Does it have any effect on when the suspension should start, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I spoke to Mr. Groome during the break and after having spoken to him, I initially thought that we could soften our position in relation to the request of a suspension, because we obviously don't want to put anyone in any inconvenience and we want the Prosecution to close their case. But the problem is that we don't have the money to hire the adequate staff to complete the tasks that remain without putting myself and the rest of the team in what we find to be unreasonable working conditions. There is obviously a reason why Defence teams have two counsel, and looking at the tasks which remain in and of themselves we could probably do them, and I am referring to the various dead-lines in terms of motions that are outstanding, and alongside preparation for the remaining witnesses. And that's what we had in mind when we asked for a suspension of the trial, other than the remaining witnesses. The procedural issues which remain, namely the motions. And the reason why we considered that -- well, I considered why we might be able to soften our position after having spoken to Mr. Groome is that we could technically manage to do those things. The problem we've got is that there are two things which we want to get on with to assist the Defence but to assist Your Honours. That's, one, to be preparing for 98 bis submissions and it to start to review the case that we can provide, well, for tomorrow a useful estimate as to what we want, but also in due course proper submissions. And the second thing is that we are still someway behind being able to analyse the Mladic diaries and the audiotapes. Whilst we were grateful for the two weeks Your Honours gave us, two weeks to analyse the audiotapes is simply -- even if we sat and listened to them without going to bed, we wouldn't get through them in two weeks. So what I'm nervous about is closing -- having the Prosecution case closed, having not considered the Mladic diaries in the depth that I would like, which might then prevents us from applying for recall of witness, if that need arises, and also in relation to the 98 bis submissions, I'm nervous that having closed the Prosecution case, Your Honours then set a deadline for the 98 bis submissions which is impossible given that we have not had the opportunity to do the type of review we would like to be doing now, which we would do if we had two counsel. So that's the dilemma we are in, we'd like to assist and close the Prosecution case and nobody more than I, but they are the problems which we can foresee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. You said the procedural issues which remain, namely the motions. No, let me see. No, I have to take another line. You told us that you didn't have the money to hire adequate staff to complete the tasks, unreasonable working conditions, and then you said: "There's obviously a reason why Defence teams have two counsel and looking at the tasks which remain in and of themselves we could probably do them, and I'm referring to the various dead-lines in terms of motions that are outstanding, and alongside preparation for the remaining witnesses. And that's what we had in mind when we asked for a suspension of the trial other than the remaining witnesses." Now, it's not entirely clear to me, did you mean to say we had in mind that we could deal with those dead-lines alongside preparation for the remaining witnesses, or did you want to say that without second counsel we could not? It's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it amounts to this, Your Honour: That if we stop all other work, we can do -- we can complete the motions. Ms. Verwiel, the principal legal assistant, is working on issues which are really important for our investigation. I've promised our investigator that we will get to her a analysis of what has happened in the courtroom because she hasn't followed all of it, and she needs to continue interviewing witnesses. If I pull Ms. Verwiel off that task then she will do the first draft of the motions then I will, while I'm preparing and cross-examining the remaining witness, find some time to finalise those responses. What won't get done is any preparation for our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear what you meant. I was just seeking clarification of your words. When I say that we have no further questions for you it doesn't mean that the matter has been entirely resolved, but we'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow the 2nd of February, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same Courtroom II.
